bullets.text: Retail oxtail for a 2024 national nutrient study came from processors in **Texas, Nebraska and Kansas**.
Each animal gives very little: USDA counts **0.24 lb of oxtail per 100 lb of live animal**.
That’s about **0.24% of live weight**, roughly 2.4 lb from a 1,000-lb steer.
The **fifth quarter** is “the non-carcass portion of a slaughtered animal”: hide, offal, tongue, **oxtail**.
The industry spec (IMPS item **721**): a “skinned tail; removed at juncture of second and third coccygeal vertebrae … cut into segments.”
Nov. 20, 2026: oxtail sold at **$595 per 100 lb**, adding **$1.43** to the **$14.17 per 100 lb** hide-and-offal value of a typical steer, about a tenth of it.

title: South Africa: oxtail on the shelf

bullets.text: The fifth quarter adds **about 5%** to an animal’s value, mostly kept by feedlots and abattoirs rather than farmers.
Tongue and oxtail are the two fifth-quarter products sold at retail. Surveyed oxtail averaged **R112.87/kg**, “comparable to mid-priced carcass cuts.”
Oxtail is “one of the world of gastronomy’s most multicultural” meats, cooked by Cubans, French, Jamaicans, Vietnamese, Chinese, Mexicans and African Americans.
Oxtail stews are “cherished comfort foods” in African and Caribbean cuisines.

**Soul food:** culinary historian Adrian Miller calls cooking with “cast-off parts,” ox tails among them, a hallmark of soul food. The same article reports oxtail was “often given to enslaved Black Americans.”

title: The Caribbean diaspora carries it north

bullets.text: In Jamaica and Guyana, oxtail is “as common as coconut bread.”
**New Jersey:** a Guyanese immigrant who first lived in **East Orange** recalls local markets starting to sell oxtail “by the late seventies or early eighties.”
**Brooklyn:** oxtail was once “almost a throwaway meat in New York.” Its price rose as Caribbean islanders settled in **Crown Heights and East Flatbush**.
2024: a Manhattan deli sells “at least 600” oxtail-stuffed patties a day.

title: From scrap to splurge: the price story

bullets.text: 2006, Brooklyn: a 15-lb box of frozen oxtail rose from about **$37 to $45** in a few months.
2015 → 2024: USDA’s average wholesale price went from **$5.99/lb to $14.19/lb**, “nearly tripled.”
Google searches for oxtail rose from a score of 6 (2004) to 73 (2024).
**Food insecurity:** in England, a participant in a 2026 study says mainstream supermarkets don’t carry her cultural foods, and “Oxtail is so expensive.”
Contrast: offal is “often more affordable than other beef cuts” and can help “resource-limited populations.”
Oxtail’s lean meat is an **“excellent source” of protein and zinc** and a **“good source” of iron and phosphorus**.
Raw oxtail lean is about **19.9% protein and 6.5% fat**, but a package is roughly **45% bone** by weight.

title: Your fork

bullets.text: Oxtail is “more commonplace in the Northeastern US.”
Close to home: Caribbean demand put oxtail in **East Orange, NJ** markets by the late 1970s–early ’80s.

story: I discovered the beauty of oxtails young as a rare commodity, it was always one of those expensive cuts for occasion. I can’t recall my very first time having oxtails but I certainly remember all the senses. Mom starting the slow crockpot at dawn, seasonings and spices filling the air around late noon, and the falling off the bone and beef stock turned to thick gravy as it was simmered. Tender, moist, and always sad when it comes to an end.
